The project charter defines a discrete unit of work that can be independently staffed and managed. The charter specifies the scope of the project and its completion criteria. It provides an agreement of what the project is committed to deliver, the budget, time constraints, resources, and standards within which it must be completed. The project charter specifies the boundary of the project – what is included and what is excluded. It also defines the required project management and control structure. The charter may be changed during the life of the project. At any time, however, it represents the agreed commitment to the parameters it defines.

The project charter must always represent the current perception of the project boundaries. The charter is used as the foundation for preparing detailed plans to be used throughout the life of the project. It also serves as a statement of the commitment of an organization to a particular project. For all these reasons, the integrity of the project charter must be preserved throughout a project. This does not mean that the charter will not or should not change; in fact, very few projects are completed without some alterations to their charters. The key point to remember is that the project must be kept on a course consistent with the boundaries specified in the charter. Any deviations from that course must be considered carefully, documented, and approved by the project sponsor through the change management process that has been established for the project.

If the client has a mature enterprise architecture practice, leverage the logical models related to BDAT (business, data, application, technology) domains to support developing the logical scope sections in the charter.

As the project progresses it is critical that either the project charter itself is updated to stay current or that it points to the most current versions of any summarized artifacts.
This artifact serves as a living document that provides the team with the background and context of the project and defines the vision of what the project is trying to achieve.

Without this artifact it will be difficult for team members to understand the purpose and overall direction of the project which may lead to misunderstandings on what needs to be done and the best way to achieve it.
On very small projects with clear objectives a simple scope statement may suffice instead of full-fledged project charter.

The project charter is a summary level document that provides a synopsis on the following aspects of the project:

  • Project goals and objectives
  • Project background and purpose
  • Clearly defined project scope (i.e., boundaries)
  • Project organization structure
  • Key stakeholders
  • Key milestones
  • Summary of critical risks, assumptions and constraints
  • High-level outline of the budget and finances
